Trading desks across the American market tracked the milestone closely, and the company reinforced its standing as one of the most watched names on the Nasdaq Composite, where its heavy weighting means each move ripples across the broader benchmark. The milestone arrived during a stretch of heavy corporate announcements and just ahead of the company's next quarterly earnings release, expected in the coming weeks. Market participants viewed the threshold as a symbolic marker of how central accelerated computing has become to the wider technology economy. The attention centres on one simple dynamic: orders for data-center hardware have continued to climb as cloud providers, enterprises and emerging model builders race to expand computing capacity. The company's accelerators remain the preferred engine for training and running large language models, and that position has translated into sustained demand across its product lines. Each new generation of chips has arrived with denser performance, prompting customers to commit to large multi-year orders of equipment and the supporting systems that surround it. Capacity has emerged as the defining constraint across the sector. Supply of advanced chips, memory and power has struggled to keep pace with demand, and lead times for new equipment have stretched considerably. The company has worked closely with foundry and memory partners to expand output, while customers plan their builds around available supply. This tight balance between supply and demand has kept pricing firm and backlogs lengthy, giving the firm visibility into orders that extends well across the coming quarters. The broader surge in demand reflects a sweeping buildout of computing infrastructure, and Nvidia sits among the most prominent names across the universe of AI Stocks tracked by market watchers. Hyperscale operators have announced enormous capital commitments to construct new data centres, and much of that spending flows toward accelerators, networking fabric and memory. These builds are not limited to established cloud giants. A new cohort of model developers, sovereign computing initiatives and specialised providers has entered the market, each seeking large allocations of high-performance chips. That diversity of demand has helped broaden the customer base beyond a handful of buyers, although a concentrated group of large customers still accounts for a sizeable share of revenue, a feature that market observers continue to weigh when assessing the durability of growth. Software has quietly become one of the firm's most valuable assets. Its programming platform has become the default framework for building and running machine-learning workloads, and a vast community of developers relies on it daily. That entrenched position gives the company influence over how applications are written, optimised and deployed across the accelerated-computing landscape, reinforcing demand for the hardware that runs best within the same ecosystem. The company has layered additional software offerings on top of this foundation, including libraries, model-serving tools and enterprise platforms sold on a subscription basis. This recurring software revenue, while small relative to hardware, adds a steadier stream and deepens customer reliance on the broader ecosystem. Market observers often point to this software moat as a defining feature of the business, one that competitors find difficult to replicate even when their silicon approaches parity on raw performance. Competition has intensified as rivals and customers alike pursue alternatives. Established chip designers have expanded their accelerator lines, while several large cloud operators have developed custom silicon to reduce reliance on any single supplier. These in-house chips aim to handle specific workloads more cheaply, and their growing presence represents a genuine headwind to the incumbent's dominance over time, particularly for tasks that do not require the full breadth of the general-purpose platform. Even so, the breadth of Nvidia's hardware-and-software combination has made wholesale switching difficult. Custom chips tend to address narrow tasks, whereas the company's platforms support a wide range of models and frameworks. The result is a market where alternatives are expanding at the margins while the incumbent retains a commanding share of the most demanding training workloads, a balance that market watchers expect to remain contested through the period ahead. Alongside the market-value milestone, the company has unveiled a steady stream of announcements spanning new chip architectures, networking systems and partnerships with governments and enterprises. These disclosures, delivered at a major developer conference held in the American capital, outlined roadmaps for coming chip generations and detailed collaborations across sectors ranging from telecommunications to scientific computing, signalling how broadly the technology is spreading beyond the familiar cloud operators. The company's reach extends across virtually every corner of the technology economy. Its chips power cloud data centres, corporate server rooms, research laboratories, gaming machines and an expanding set of automotive and robotics platforms. This breadth means demand is not tied to a single end market, giving the firm multiple avenues of growth even as the data-center segment dominates the current revenue mix. Each of these end markets carries its own cycle, and the diversity helps smooth the swings that can accompany any one of them. The milestone unfolded against a backdrop of elevated enthusiasm for artificial-intelligence names across the American equity market. Several of the largest technology firms now carry outsized weightings in major benchmarks, and movements in these shares can sway the broader . That concentration has drawn commentary about how dependent headline indices have become on a small group of megacap names, with the chipmaker among the most influential of them. Sentiment toward the sector has swung between exuberance and caution, with some market participants questioning whether the pace of capital spending can be sustained. Nvidia's trajectory carries implications far beyond its own balance sheet. As the dominant supplier of accelerated-computing hardware, its order patterns serve as a barometer for the health of the broader artificial-intelligence buildout. Equipment makers, memory producers, networking firms and power providers all take cues from the company's demand signals, making its results a reference point for an entire supply chain that stretches from raw silicon to finished data centres. Several uncertainties hang over the story. Export restrictions affecting sales to certain overseas markets have already trimmed addressable demand, and shifts in trade rules could alter the picture further. The company has navigated these constraints by adjusting product configurations, yet the regulatory environment remains fluid and difficult to map with precision, leaving a measure of uncertainty around how much of the global market stays open. Demand concentration is another consideration. A handful of large customers account for a meaningful portion of revenue, so any slowdown in their spending would be felt quickly. Questions about whether the current pace of data-center construction can continue indefinitely add a further layer of uncertainty that market watchers weigh against the strong order book and the company's expanding roster of customers. The company's next quarterly earnings release is expected in the coming weeks, and it will offer the clearest read yet on whether demand remains as strong as recent commentary implies. Revenue trends in the data-center segment, gross-margin behaviour and guidance for the coming quarters will all draw close scrutiny from market participants seeking confirmation that growth has not begun to cool after such a prolonged ascent. Each quarterly release from the firm has become a major event for the wider market, given its heavy index weighting and its role as a proxy for artificial-intelligence demand. Looking to the period ahead, the company faces the twin tasks of sustaining supply growth and defending its ecosystem against rising competition. Its roadmap points to continued performance gains with each chip generation, and its software moat remains a formidable barrier to entry. How well it manages capacity, pricing and customer concentration will shape the next chapter of the story and determine how durable the recent momentum proves to be. title: Anthropic's IPO Filing Reveals a Massive Opportunity for AI Infrastructure Giants - MarketBeat
content:
The foundational artificial intelligence landscape shifted on Oct. 26, 2026, when Anthropic publicly filed its initial public offering prospectus. This highly anticipated debut, expected to price in mid-November under the Nasdaq ticker symbol ANT, offers a rare look under the hood of a leading generative artificial intelligence developer. For investors unable to participate in the upcoming offering, the filing offers an immediate, actionable proxy. The underlying numbers suggest Anthropic's S-1 functions less as a traditional equity debut and more as an approximately $221 billion verified purchase order for the broader infrastructure sector. By exposing non-cancelable compute agreements, the prospectus confirms that the primary beneficiaries of generative AI scale remain the hyperscalers and semiconductor sector giants supplying the backend architecture. Anthropic generated an impressive $16.3 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026. That figure sits alongside an $80.7 billion net loss. A cursory glance might suggest an unsustainable cash burn rate, but a balance sheet analysis tells a vastly different story. Most of that $80.7 billion deficit is an accounting artifact: a non-cash charge driven by mark-to-market adjustments to derivative liabilities. When early investors provided capital via convertible instruments, the rapid appreciation of the private valuation forced Anthropic to mark those liabilities higher, recognizing the difference as a net loss on the income statement. Amazon's second-quarter 2026 results previously previewed this phenomenon, featuring a $53.4 billion non-operating gain tied almost entirely to the Amazon stake in Anthropic. These figures reflect structural valuation shifts rather than operational cash depletion, allowing investors to focus on underlying revenue growth and the infrastructure needed to sustain it. Understanding this non-cash mechanism prevents misinterpreting the figure as operational cash burn and keeps the focus squarely on foundational hardware demand. One of the most revealing metrics buried within the filing is not the equity valuation but the scale of the vendor commitments. Anthropic secured roughly $110 billion in non-cancelable cloud compute agreements with Amazon and $114.5 billion with Alphabet. These agreements function as long-term spending commitments that provide substantial revenue visibility for Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud infrastructure over the coming years. Amazon and Alphabet occupy a unique, vertically integrated position within the generative artificial intelligence ecosystem. Both companies operate simultaneously as principal investors funding the foundational models, primary compute suppliers servicing those models, and direct competitors developing rival platforms. Strategic investments in this space function as enclosed ecosystems, where institutional capital injections recycle back into the investors' cloud divisions via binding compute contracts. The critical fundamental question is how these top-line guarantees flow through to cloud operating margins and free cash flow. While the revenue is secured, servicing an excess of $220 billion in compute demand requires aggressive capital expenditure cycles. With both Amazon and Alphabet scheduled to report earnings this week, management commentary regarding capital expenditures and anticipated infrastructure amortization schedules will serve as immediate catalysts. Investors might watch these reports closely for signs of cloud margin expansion, which would validate the profitability of recycling venture investments back into enclosed compute contracts. Tracing these locked-in cloud expenditures down the hardware stack reveals the secondary layer of beneficiaries. Hyperscalers cannot service an approximately $221 billion compute mandate without expanding their physical data center footprints, which translates directly to component demand. This capital outlay flows through a dual-track architecture pipeline. A large portion of the compute load relies on merchant silicon, reinforcing NVIDIA's NASDAQ: NVDA data-center dominance. As the primary architect of the advanced graphics processing units powering generative artificial intelligence training clusters, NVIDIA remains positioned to capture the immediate hardware spend. NVIDIA, trading at a premium valuation and closing in on a $5.25 trillion market capitalization, relies on these entrenched, multi-year hyperscaler commitments to maintain earnings momentum. This shift toward proprietary architecture channels substantial revenue streams toward Broadcom NASDAQ: AVGO, which co-designs and supplies the networking components and custom application-specific integrated circuits necessary for these hyperscaler deployments. Broadcom's fundamental narrative anchors heavily to this custom silicon demand, making the Anthropic scale-up a direct structural tailwind for both semiconductor leaders. While the infrastructure beneficiaries appear insulated by binding contracts, the prospectus explicitly flags the inherent vulnerabilities of standalone foundational model developers. Heavy customer concentration stands out as a primary risk factor, as Anthropic relies on a narrow base of enterprise clients for revenue. More complex is the paradox of relying on the same entities that act as direct competitors. Securing raw compute power from Amazon and Alphabet means the operational backbone is controlled by the organizations building rival foundational platforms. These non-cancelable compute agreements secure necessary capacity but lock Anthropic into rigid cost structures, limiting flexibility if hardware pricing dynamics shift. Board and executive leadership must navigate structural conflicts of interest, since the entities providing the necessary infrastructure also hold significant ownership stakes. The eventual pricing of the upcoming offering will set a critical benchmark for the entire sector. Without a set share count or valuation range officially disclosed ahead of the reported mid-November debut, the broader market is waiting to see how institutional capital prices high-revenue generative artificial intelligence models burdened by high infrastructure costs. The structural realities detailed in the prospectus reinforce the thesis that the most predictable revenue streams in the artificial intelligence sector currently reside within the physical infrastructure layer. Investors monitoring the space may view the upcoming mega-cap technology earnings as the immediate proving ground for this view. If Amazon and Alphabet demonstrate that high capital investments translate into expanding cloud operating margins, the fundamental case for the underlying semiconductor suppliers strengthens. Cautious investors may prefer to observe how the hyperscalers manage their capital expenditure forecasts before adjusting their exposure to the hardware providers powering the generative transition. title: Jensen Huang Says Nvidia's Next-Gen Vera Rubin Chips Will Generate $40 Billion in Revenue per Gigawatt, Up From $25 Billion for Grace Blackwell. What That Means for NVDA's Growth Runway. - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia says each gigawatt of AI capacity is now worth 60% more to it with Vera Rubin, and that could extend its growth runway even if customers don't add more power. Nvidia (NVDA +2.39%) has already made an incredible amount of money selling the powerful chips that drive artificial intelligence (AI). But CEO Jensen Huang believes the company's biggest opportunities are still ahead, and Nvidia's newest technology could help him prove it. The chipmaker's next-generation Vera Rubin architecture is designed to deliver substantially more computing power from the same amount of electricity. That's important for cloud companies that are racing to build AI data centers, where access to power has become a major constraint. But there's another benefit for Nvidia shareholders. Vera Rubin could generate 60% more revenue per gigawatt of computing capacity than its predecessor. And that helps explain why Huang is so confident about Nvidia's growth runway. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images. Nvidia's Hopper and Blackwell graphics processing units (GPUs) have been enormously successful with hyperscalers and smaller cloud providers building artificial intelligence computing capacity. But Nvidia isn't simply selling faster GPUs anymore. Its Vera Rubin platform combines Rubin GPUs, Vera central processing units (CPUs), high-speed NVLink connections, networking equipment, and software into a complete AI computing system. NVLink enables processors to communicate and share memory access more efficiently, helping customers complete more computing work without a corresponding increase in electricity consumption. During Nvidia's fiscal second-quarter 2027 earnings call in August, Huang explained how that expanding platform translates into a bigger revenue opportunity. "In the case of Hopper, we were at about $18 billion per gigawatt. For Grace Blackwell, we're at about $25 billion per gigawatt. And for Vera Rubin, it's about $40 billion per gigawatt," he said. "And the productivity is X-factors increase in each generation." That's a 60% increase over Blackwell, even if customers don't build any additional power capacity. And the technology is already moving into the market. Nvidia says Vera Rubin has entered production shipments, with purchase orders from major hyperscalers, AI cloud providers, and equipment manufacturers. Huang predicted last year that AI infrastructure spending could reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030, and he reiterated that forecast in September. He's also expecting Nvidia to sell twice as many chips in 2027 as in 2026, according to comments he made to reporters in Scotland on Sept. 17. That doesn't necessarily mean Nvidia's revenue will double. Chip volumes and revenue are different measurements, and the $40 billion-per-gigawatt figure represents a potential sales opportunity rather than guaranteed orders. But the underlying business is already growing at an extraordinary pace. Nvidia reported $96.2 billion in revenue for its fiscal second quarter, which ended July 26, up 106% from a year earlier. Data center revenue alone reached $89 billion. Vera Rubin gives Nvidia another way to increase revenue beyond simply selling more GPUs. If customers continue to expand their AI capacity while spending more per gigawatt on Nvidia technology, the company's growth runway could be considerably longer than its already massive size suggests. title: Questions Arise Over Neoclouds’ Operational Stability, Testing NVIDIA’s (NVDA.US) Role as an AI Financier - 富途牛牛
content: NVIDIA (NVDA.US) stated that, as credit markets tighten for its major partners, the company's role as a global financier of AI infrastructure is facing its first major stress test. After launching relevant chips in the early stages of generative AI, NVIDIA began leveraging its financial strength to provide funding support to AI model developers, data center companies, and several so‑called neoclouds (new cloud service providers). CEO Jensen Huang's strategy, in addition to building cutting‑edge technology, also involves offering customers investment and loan assistance to promote broader adoption of the systems. The arrangements include leveraging NVIDIA's investment-grade credit rating to provide guarantees for OpenAI's large-scale projects, enabling the related construction to secure financing at lower interest rates. As of the most recent quarterly financial filing in July, NVIDIA has entered into off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements or guarantees involving neoclouds totaling $36 billion, and it has also provided up to $105 billion in guarantees for chips, land, and electricity related to OpenAI's plan to build a 10-gigawatt data center in Ohio. The company has also signed $20 billion in future data center leases, which it will subsequently transfer to third parties. Under most transactions, NVIDIA is only liable for payment if the project participants default. David Trainer, founder and CEO of the financial research firm New Constructs, stated that if computing power demand fails to meet the market's extremely high expectations, problems will arise. Market conditions may test NVIDIA's resilience. In NVIDIA's portfolio, neoclouds such as CoreWeave (CRWV.US), Nebius (NBIS.US), and IREN (IREN.US)—all of which continue to burn cash—have all seen their stock prices plunge by at least 30% this month. Among them, the largest, CoreWeave, has seen its credit default swap spread rise above 11%, reflecting that investors must pay higher premiums to guard against default. Other neoclouds backed by NVIDIA are also facing challenges. The company is an investor in Firmus, an Australian AI cloud provider, which abruptly withdrew its IPO plans this month; UK-based Nscale and SB Energy, which is supported by SoftBank, also filed to list in the U.S. in September, but there has been no update on their progress for several weeks. Last week, Jensen Huang reiterated his confidence in the market, telling CNBC that demand for neoclouds is "extremely strong." During an interview with CNBC at the GTC conference in Berlin, Huang noted that what's currently lacking is working capital to support growth, as surging demand across multiple AI sectors has led to a shortage of available capital. NVIDIA has invested in dozens of companies, including substantial stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic. As of the second quarter, its investment portfolio was valued at $99 billion. Investors told CNBC that the market is watching how NVIDIA will use its cash and its $5 trillion market capitalization to deliver more chips to customers, as well as how much risk the company is willing to take. Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said that market volatility reflects investors' concerns about business stability. He noted that CoreWeave and other neoclouds enter into long-term contracts; while their earnings reports appear promising, the market is focused on whether these contracts can remain stable. title: Is Nvidia Stock Cheaper Now That Its Multiple Has Fallen? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Many investors evaluate NVIDIA (NVDA) the way they evaluate any stock: the lower the price-to-earnings multiple, the cheaper the stock. That multiple, what investors pay for each dollar of profit, stood at 101.3 for Nvidia in mid-2023. Today it is 26.5. Does a multiple that has fallen this far mean you are getting a cheaper stock? Nvidia’s share price rose 398.7% from mid-2023 to October 23, 2026, excluding dividends. A single share now costs far more than it did, while each dollar of profit behind it costs far less. Over the same three years, the price went up and the multiple went down. Nvidia’s profit over the latest twelve months reached $193 billion, compared with $10.3 billion in the twelve months to mid-2023. That is 18.7 times as much profit in three years. The table below shows how profit and the multiple moved year by year. Net income is the reported total for the twelve months ending on the date shown. Change in a year compares that net income to the twelve months prior. Each price-to-earnings multiple divides the market value at the calendar quarter end paired with those twelve months by the net income for those twelve months; the final row uses the share price of Oct 23, 2026. Nvidia generates its sales mostly from one business: the Compute & Networking segment made up 89.6% of revenue in fiscal 2026. On the August 26, 2026 call, management said a surge in AI demand is driving a global infrastructure buildout, and that sustained strength in Blackwell drove sales to hyperscale customers. Not in the way the rule suggests. A better question is what investors were paying for when the multiple was high. Nvidia’s multiple peaked at 143.1 in early 2023, when twelve-month profit had dipped to about $4.8 billion. Profit today is about 40 times that. Investors paid the most for each dollar of profit when there was far less of it because they expected it to grow, and it did. Today, a buyer pays less for each dollar of profit than a buyer did three years ago. That earlier buyer was paying for growth that has since happened. The lower multiple partly reflects growth that has already arrived, so it is not by itself a discount. This follows the usual curve for a fast grower: the multiple is highest while the profit is still expected, and lower once it is here. Nvidia’s profit is still growing fast, and it is expanding faster than it did a year earlier. Profit rose 122.7% in the latest twelve months, compared with 63.4% the year before. Profit also grew faster than sales, which rose 83.4%. Nvidia’s multiple today sits above the S&P 500’s 22.9. When Nvidia reports in November 2026, the figure to watch is whether profit keeps growing near the latest year’s pace. title: Nvidia vs. Micron: The AI Revolution Is Big Enough for Both. Here's the Better Buy. - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia (NVDA +2.39%) and Micron (MU +2.98%) each have been playing key roles in the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Nvidia is the maker of the logic chip that powers the "thinking" of AI models, while Micron makes the memory and storage solutions that are also essential in the training and use of AI. Investors have recognized the importance of these companies and their products and have piled into their shares. Nvidia's gains started earlier than those of Micron, back in 2023, and have accelerated over the past two years. Micron climbed somewhat back then but truly took off this year. Over the past five years, Nvidia has advanced more than 800%, while Micron has soared 1,200%. The AI revolution is big enough for both of these market titans -- but which is the better buy? Let's find out. Nvidia dominates the AI chip market, selling the graphics processing units (GPUs) that power unavoidable tasks such as the training and inference of models. The company isn't alone in the market, but it is the leader thanks to its early entry, the speed of its GPUs, and its commitment to innovation to remain ahead of rivals. All of this has translated into eye-popping earnings growth over the past few years. Nvidia's revenue and profit have marched higher, climbing in the double and triple digits to record levels. In the latest period, for example, revenue soared 106% to $96 billion, while net income jumped 126% to $59 billion. Though Nvidia is best known for its GPUs, the company's work doesn't stop here. It has created complete systems, including networking tools and enterprise software, and developed platforms to serve specific industries like healthcare and robotics. The tech giant has also been growing its presence through acquisitions as we can see through its plan to buy open-source AI platform Hugging Face. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » As the AI focus transitions from the training of models to widespread use of AI in the real world, Nvidia is well positioned to benefit and continue delivering solid revenue gains. Micron has served the AI market in its early days, for the training of models, but the greater revenue opportunity is happening now and may continue well into the future. As mentioned, the company makes the memory and storage needed for various AI tasks. And the current and future major revenue opportunity lies in the area of agentic AI. This involves AI taking on a problem and going through various steps to solve it. And for this, memory is needed on an ongoing basis, representing significant and lasting growth for Micron. This is why, with the market moving toward agentic AI, Micron's earnings and stock price have surged. In the latest quarter, the company reported a revenue increase of more than 370%, and with memory supply tight, Micron has developed strategic customer agreements or multi-year supply contracts. This move secures supply for customers into the future and offers Micron and its shareholders greater visibility into revenue to come. So these agreements are positive for all involved. Considering we're in the early stages of the use of AI in the real world, Micron's revenue could continue to march higher in the quarters to come. Nvidia and Micron are both important players in the AI revolution. And today, each of these stocks looks reasonably priced. But the better buy today is Nvidia. Here's why. Micron should continue to generate growth, but it is more vulnerable to a potential decline in prices once memory supply normalizes over the next couple of years. And this could weigh on growth. The memory market is cyclical, shifting from periods of tight supply to oversupply -- and an eventual time of high supply is likely to slow or halt Micron's momentum. Nvidia, due to its broad presence across the AI industry and range of products and services, might better navigate potential headwinds -- and feel less pressure on earnings and stock performance. The company's market isn't cyclical, which means greater stability in revenue over time. All of this means Nvidia is the best stock to add to your AI portfolio right now. title: Apollo finds no broad AI payoff: NVDA stock forecast before earnings - Techi
content: Apollo sees little AI payoff beyond big tech. TECHi finds Nvidia’s EPS estimate held steady while NVDA’s forward multiple fell 6%, then maps conditional prices before earnings. Illustrative data-center racks, not a verified NVIDIA facility. Photo by Brett Sayles / Pexels, used under the Pexels License; cropped and toned by TECHi. Apollo's chief economist argued in an October 24 research note that broad US companies still show little measurable financial payoff from artificial intelligence. That is a warning about the economics of the buyers at the far end of the AI chain, not a new earnings report from Nvidia. For NVDA holders, the immediate question is whether the market will lower the price it pays for Nvidia's expected earnings before those earnings themselves turn down. There is already a measurable gap. From September 24 to the October 23 close, TECHi's NVDA forecast data show the same-period FY2027 EPS estimate edging from $9.3071 to $9.3124, while the share price fell from $224.58 to $210.96. TECHi calculates a 0.06% estimate increase against a 6.06% price decline. The implied price-to-estimated-earnings ratio slipped from about 24.13 to 22.65. That compression, rather than a documented collapse in Nvidia profit expectations, is the starting point for this forecast. Our calculation uses two dated observations of the same fiscal-year EPS estimate and the corresponding daily closes. The September 24 observation shows $224.58 divided by $9.3071, or 24.13 times. The October 23 close of $210.96 divided by $9.3124 yields 22.65 times. The ratio fell roughly 6.12%; EPS changed by less than one tenth of one percent. These are estimates and historical market prices from TECHi's data providers, not audited FY2027 results. Price adjustments were not confirmed by the quote page, and the estimate date's close is not necessarily the price at the exact moment the estimate was issued. The distinction matters because a valuation multiple is the market's willingness to pay for a dollar of forecast earnings. It can shrink when investors ask whether end customers will ultimately earn enough on AI to sustain infrastructure spending, even while current orders remain strong. Apollo's note gives that question a new data frame: it compares revenue per worker and profit margins for the seven biggest technology companies with the other 493 S&P 500 constituents and finds improvement concentrated in the tech group. Apollo also points to a productivity series and token-spending data. Its argument is about broad diffusion of AI benefits, not a census of every business using Nvidia hardware. Apollo's language is forceful, but the evidence supports a narrower investor conclusion than "AI demand has ended." Flat aggregate margins outside big tech cannot identify which individual firms used AI, when they adopted it, what they paid, or whether a particular project saved costs. A benefit can also arrive with a lag or be competed away in lower prices. The S&P 493 comparison is a reason to scrutinize the next layer of spending and pricing; it is not proof that Nvidia's next reported quarter will miss guidance. Nvidia's own August 26 results provide the counterweight. Revenue for the quarter ended July 26 was $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier. Data Center revenue reached $89.0 billion, up 117%. Using the more precise figures in its Form 10-Q, Data Center supplied about 92.5% of total quarterly revenue: $89.023 billion divided by $96.221 billion. This is a company whose current sales are deeply tied to the AI buildout, regardless of what Apollo's economy-wide charts say about customers' current returns. The company guided for fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, and a 74.0% gross margin, plus or minus 0.5 percentage point. The revenue midpoint is about 12.2% above the July quarter's $96.221 billion. Guidance is a management forecast, not a result. Nvidia specifically excluded Data Center compute revenue from China in that outlook. A quarter near the midpoint would show that equipment demand remained robust through the reporting period, though it would not establish that enterprises buying AI services are themselves earning attractive returns. The route from enterprise budgets to Nvidia revenue is indirect. Nvidia sells to manufacturers, integrators, cloud providers, AI labs and others; a business can rent computing from a cloud provider rather than purchase Nvidia systems itself. The 10-Q says one direct customer accounted for 16% of second-quarter revenue. Nvidia also estimates that one AI research and deployment company contributed a meaningful amount of revenue by purchasing cloud services from its customers. It does not name that indirect customer in this disclosure. Investor exposure therefore depends on a chain of customers' funding, utilization and pricing decisions, not a single chart of non-tech corporate margins. There is a plausible delay between Apollo's concern and a chipmaker's results. Hyperscalers may continue building capacity already ordered or contracted even if some enterprise customers are still testing applications. AI labs may use more compute to train and serve models before the broader economy shows a productivity gain. Conversely, a long spell of poor downstream returns can eventually limit customers' willingness to pay, weaken cloud pricing and slow the next round of equipment orders. The investment question is the timing and strength of that feedback loop. Friday's $210.96 regular-session close on October 23 is the price baseline; US shares do not trade in their regular session on Saturday. TECHi's earnings calendar lists November 17, 2026 after market close as the next confirmed Nvidia report. The following are TECHi valuation sensitivities around that event, not analyst targets, probabilities, or a claim that these prices will trade on November 18. Each calculation starts from the October 24 FY2027 EPS estimate of $9.3124 shown on TECHi's forecast page and changes only the multiple. Results are rounded to cents after multiplication. The spread between $167.62 and $242.12 is $74.50 per share with the EPS input held fixed. That width shows how sensitive an expensive growth stock can be to the narrative about future demand. It does not measure expected volatility or substitute for an options market estimate. TECHi's live forecast page displays a mean analyst target of $328.95, but that target has an unspecified horizon and target sample count; it is neither a November target nor the source of our three cases. A more direct way to read the model is to ask what multiple the market assigns after seeing the next report. If Nvidia reports near its $108 billion revenue midpoint and around the guided 74% gross margin, investors could still refuse to restore September's 24.13-times multiple if downstream ROI remains uncertain. At the current $9.3124 estimate, 24.13 times would imply roughly $224.72, about 6.5% above Friday's close. That is the amount of valuation recovery required merely to revisit September's multiple using today's slightly higher EPS estimate. The earnings report can change the EPS input as well, so this calculation should not be read as a price target. Apollo's research is most useful as a testable warning. The bearish feedback loop would become more persuasive if cloud providers reported weaker AI-service pricing or utilization, if large buyers deferred infrastructure commitments, or if Nvidia's own guidance and gross margin fell below its August outlook. A broad-market productivity chart alone would not establish any of those company-specific developments. Nvidia's filings also identify power availability, land, capital and deployment constraints as reasons customers may postpone purchases; even healthy end demand could be delayed by physical infrastructure. The bullish counterargument is substantial. Nvidia has already shown extraordinary reported revenue growth, a 75% July-quarter gross margin, and a $108 billion next-quarter revenue midpoint. Management expects to sell both Blackwell and Rubin systems and says supply constraints remain. Demand can stay ahead of supply for a time even when average enterprise ROI is unclear. Strong cloud contracts, better utilization and pricing, or profitable deployment by customers would weaken Apollo's concern and support a higher multiple. None of those outcomes can be inferred from share-price movement alone. There is also a risk of measuring the wrong end of the chain. Apollo's S&P 493 series asks whether ordinary listed companies are seeing higher revenue per employee or margins. Nvidia's near-term customers include cloud and AI firms that may sell capacity to startups and enterprises worldwide. The public S&P 493 is not the full set of Nvidia's end users. Its companies also differ in accounting, sector mix and spending cycles. Treat Apollo's aggregate result as a challenge to the long-run AI demand thesis, not a substitute for Nvidia's reported sales or the next round of customer disclosures. For a holder deciding what to watch next, the order is practical. The October 26 market open will show how investors first price Apollo's dated research after the weekend; there is no Saturday regular-session NVDA move to report. Then the November 17 earnings release will test the $108 billion revenue midpoint, the 74% gross-margin guide, and management's comments on customer mix and capacity. Afterward, updates from the large cloud buyers will help determine whether rented AI compute is turning into durable, profitable demand. The forecast changes if those observations move the EPS estimate or justify a different multiple. Until then, the most defensible reading is that Nvidia's earnings expectations have held up far better than its valuation since late September. title: Elon Musk Just Gave Fantastic News for Nvidia Investors - The Motley Fool
content: The new SpaceX SI data center cluster is going to run on the Nvidia Vera Rubin computer. Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -0.40%) just reported fabulous earnings, with a 161% increase in revenue and a $4.4 billion net income, its first quarterly profit. Elon Musk shared exciting news about where the company's headed, including perfecting reusable spaceships and increasing satellite bandwidth by 100x.  But he also gave fabulous news for Nvidia (NVDA +2.39%) investors. The standout in the report was the artificial intelligence (AI) business, now called SI, or Super Intelligence. Sales rose an astonishing 835% year over year, driven by compute deals, the acquisition of coding company Cursor, and enterprise adoption of the Grok AI model. It also became profitable, with $431 million in operating income. Musk boasted that he took the same team that made SpaceX's rocket business so dominant and tasked them with deploying AI compute infrastructure, likening it to "the New York Yankees playing in Little League" and calling it "not fair" to the competition. The company rents out compute power from its massive Colossus I data center cluster, and it has agreements with Alphabet and Anthropic for $920 million and $1.2 billion in monthly revenue, respectively. It's now in the process of building Colossus II, and Musk said that it will predominantly feature Nvidia's Vera Rubin chip infrastructure. He also said that SI plans "to have the most powerful training cluster online" by the second quarter, and to that end, it will need "440,000 Vera Rubin computers deployed for optimal training." Grok is growing quickly, with accelerating usage, and SpaceX is scaling it for enterprises. Musk sees them using Grok Bot, its AI agent, in roles as if it were a human agent. "I've never seen anything grow this fast," he said, and he anticipates Grok Bot being the main user of the extra compute. Musk thinks that SpaceX could have $500 billion to $1 trillion in Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) by the end of 2027. If so, that would make it one of the biggest companies in the world by sales. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang gave a forecast of $1 trillion in sales through 2027 from the Blackwell and Rubin lines alone, and CFO Collette Kress said the company expects sales to increase 70% next year, although that's in a supply-constrained climate. Wall Street expects Nvidia sales to reach $692 billion next year, and that's with a 68% increase. I would also note that Musk specifically said he's going to use Vera Rubin computers, not just Rubin chips. That's a full-stack computer system that brings in more revenue than chips alone. That's great news for Nvidia and its shareholders, and it implies that there's still major upside for Nvidia stock over the next few years. title: Apple Joins Nvidia in the $5 Trillion Club. Here's Which Stock I Think Can Get to $10 Trillion First. - The Motley Fool
content: One company serves corporations in a cyclical, increasingly competitive business environment. The other serves consumers who are loyal regardless of the economic backdrop. Apple (AAPL -1.10%) was the first company to reach a $1 trillion market cap, way back in 2018. Thanks to the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence, however, hardware maker Nvidia (NVDA +2.39%) became the world's first $5 trillion outfit late last year. Now Apple's turning heads again. Thanks to its stock's recent gains, it joined the $5 trillion club just last week. Nvidia is still technically bigger, albeit barely, with its current market cap of $5.13 trillion. This market cap movement prompts a question: Although it doesn't really matter, which of these two companies is more likely to reach a $10 trillion valuation first? I suspect it's going to be Apple. Here's why. Nvidia is still a fine growth investment. Even if we don't know exactly what the future holds, we can confidently say that computing technology -- including artificial intelligence -- features prominently in it. That bodes well for this tech giant. There's a reason NVDA shares are priced relatively cheaply at just 14 times next year's expected per-share profit of $15.91, though. That is -- perhaps without even consciously realizing it -- the market is pricing in a headwind for Nvidia's AI business. It may also be factoring in the recent rise of AI computing competitors like Advanced Micro Devices and Qualcomm. It's a potential problem because data centers alone now account for roughly 90% of Nvidia's revenue. But isn't Apple an artificial intelligence company too? Not really. While Apple's iPhone and its iOS certainly offer artificial intelligence-based solutions to their users, these are features rather than the crux of these profit centers. Most iPhone owners -- who consistently account for about half of Apple's sales -- simply prefer this particular smartphone for the overall experience it provides. They loved it well before AI was part of it. And that's the key to this ticker's market-beating past, present, and projected growth. It's not a hardware company in the same sense that Nvidia provides technology to institutions that perpetually shop for the most bang for their computing buck (so to speak). Rather, Apple is a lifestyle brand that's fostered enormous loyalty from a consumer market that's already more reliable and predictable than the corporate arena. Consumer Intelligence Research Partners reports that 87% of current iPhone owners say their next smartphone purchase will be another iPhone, explaining the ongoing growth in the number of Apple-made devices actively used worldwide. The company reported this figure reached a new record of 2.5 billion early this year. Knowing the sort of future growth performance they're almost certainly plugging into, investors have also consistently supported a premium valuation for Apple stock. It's possible the underlying dynamic here could change in unexpected ways, pushing Nvidia to the $10 trillion mark before Apple gets there. And it doesn't really matter which one reaches the milestone first. Still, if nothing else, comparing and contrasting what makes these two companies tick is an important thought exercise that helps all investors establish reasonable expectations. Just keep in mind that both stocks can perform more than well enough going forward. James Brumley has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. title: Prediction: $200 a Month Invested in Nvidia Will Be Worth This Much by 2035 - The Motley Fool
content: Small but steady investments in the chipmaker could build a meaningful position by 2035. Putting aside $200 to invest every month is not something everyone can do. Yet for those who can and do, the potential rewards are real. If you start next month and continue through December 2035, you'll have put aside $22,000 in contributions alone. But along the way, if you put that money into the right investments -- for example, Nvidia (NVDA +2.39%) -- those contributions could grow into a much larger nest egg. But what's a realistic return to expect from that strategy over the next nine years, especially given how much Nvidia stock has already grown recently? The answer starts with Nvidia's business model and ends with how much investors are willing to pay for its future. Imagine it's 2035. Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots have moved from the fringes to everyday use. Scheduling an appointment? You'll almost certainly be talking to an AI chatbot. At the drive-thru? An AI chatbot might take your latte order. Have a question about your taxes? There will likely be an AI chatbot for that. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » In short, AI isn't going anywhere. In fact, as the systems improve, organizations will rely more on AI-powered tools to stay competitive and meet consumer expectations for speed, accuracy, and 24/7 availability. To power these applications, AI hyperscalers will need a far greater number of expensive graphics processing units (GPUs), the brains of the latest and greatest AI applications. Or as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently said, "AI has reached its inflection point." What Huang means by this is that AI systems are increasingly moving from learning about the world (training) to problem-solving (inference). As we move forward, these systems will be able to handle increasingly difficult tasks, often independently once they've received their initial instructions. Based on that, we can expect AI to follow a path similar to the ones previously charted by technologies such as electricity, telecommunications, and the internet: evolving from a novelty we marvel at to an engine of rapid growth, and ultimately becoming an essential utility. Putting aside $200 per month adds up to $2,400 per year. Do that for just over nine straight years (110 months), and you end up with $22,000 just from contributions. To plot what that might turn into over time, let's look at several paths forward, running from bearish to bullish. At the low end, if Nvidia endures a negative 5% annualized return, you'd end up with a position worth $17,677. On the other hand, the total skyrockets to more than $61,930 with a 20% annualized return. For context, Nvidia has averaged an eye-popping 63% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over the last 10 years. But given that it's now the world's largest company, accounting for about 7% of the value of the entire U.S. stock market all by itself, it's unreasonable to think that it could repeat that type of performance over the next decade. There are two obvious threats that could put hurdles in the way of Nvidia's growth. First, regardless of demand, the company might not actually be able to source enough components or production capacity to deliver fully on that demand. On the latest earnings call, Huang noted that "our entire supply chain is challenged." Ultimately, Nvidia can only grow as fast as its suppliers and foundry partners allow, and if the supply chain begins to bend and creak under the enormous weight of the AI revolution, that could slow Nvidia's growth. NVDA Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts. Second, Nvidia's customers and competitors (which in some cases are the same companies) might alter their courses. AI hyperscalers are spending enormous amounts of money building out AI infrastructure at breakneck speed. If one or more were to pull back on spending, Nvidia's top line could take a hit. Similarly, rising competition could begin to erode Nvidia's margins. Direct rivals like AMD are gaining ground with new products, and even Nvidia's largest customers like Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft are investing heavily in developing their own AI chips in partnership with players like Broadcom and Marvell Technology. For argument's sake, let's say that Nvidia could deliver a 10% annualized return over the next 110 months. At that rate, the total value of your position would grow to just over $35,000. This growth rate assumes Nvidia will face continued supply chain challenges, but not catastrophic ones. It also assumes that, even as competition continues to increase, Nvidia will maintain a significant competitive advantage in data center processors. In summary, the $200/month habit is entirely controllable; the results are not. Nonetheless, a person who consistently invests is already paying their future self and is likely to be rewarded. Even if Nvidia falls well short of its recent returns, a market-matching 10% return would still deliver significant benefits. title: Nvidia's role as AI financier faces first big test as neoclouds take market hit - CNBC
content:
Nvidia’s emergence as financier for the global AI buildout is facing its first major stress test as credit markets tighten for key partners. After creating the chips that powered the early stages of the generative artificial intelligence era, Nvidia turned to using its financial prowess to fund AI model developers, data center companies and a host of so-called neoclouds. CEO Jensen Huang’s strategy has been to not only build the most advanced technology but to provide customers with investment as well as help them take out loans so his systems can reach many more hands. That’s meant taking full advantage of Nvidia’s investment grade credit rating and providing backstop guarantees on mega-projects for OpenAI so that buildouts can get funded at lower interest rates. As of its last quarterly financial filing in July, Nvidia had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, in addition to its guarantee on up to $105 billion for chips, land and power at a proposed 10 gigawatt OpenAI data center in Ohio. The company signed as a tenant for $20 billion in future data center leases, which will later be assigned to third parties. For the vast majority of these deals, Nvidia won’t have to pay up unless participants in the project default. “If the demand for compute doesn’t meet these really super lofty expectations, we’re going to have a problem,” said David Trainer, founder and CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, in an interview. Market conditions may soon test Nvidia’s mettle. Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, all cash-burning companies in Nvidia’s portfolio, are down at least 30% this month. CoreWeave, the biggest of the group, has seen the spread on its credit default swaps soar past 11%, as investors are forced to pay up for insurance against default. Nvidia has backed other neoclouds that have run into challenges. The company is an investor in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus, which abruptly withdrew its IPO plans this month, as well as Nscale out of the U.K. and SoftBank-backed SB Energy. Both of those companies filed to go public in the U.S. in September but haven’t provided updates on their plans in weeks. Nvidia wrapped up a third straight down week on Wall Street on Friday, with its stock now off 7.6% in October, on pace for its worst month since November of last year. Huang reiterated his confidence in the market this week, telling CNBC on Thursday that demand for neoclouds is “off the charts.” “What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth,” Huang told CNBC’s Arjun Kharpal on the sidelines of the company’s GTC conference in Berlin. “Because there’s just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there’s a scarcity of capital.” Nvidia has taken equity stakes in dozens of companies, including big investments in OpenAI and Anthropic. Its portfolio is worth $99 billion as of the second quarter. Investors told CNBC that a big question surrounding Nvidia is how the company can use its cash and $5 trillion market cap to get more chips into customers’ hands, and how much risk it will assume in the process. Nvidia graphics processing units are critical for training and deploying AI models. Revenue in the latest fiscal year hit $216 billion, up roughly eightfold since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022. Before the AI boom, Nvidia sold graphics cards that could fit into a standard server rack or PC. Its newest systems are much larger and more expensive. Nvidia’s flagship Vera Rubin product is a seven-foot rack containing 72 GPUs and weighing as much as a pickup truck. It costs more than $7 million, according to a Morgan Stanley estimate. While Nvidia still dominates the AI chip market, competition is emerging from the likes of Google, which rents out tensor processing units (TPUs) inside its massive cloud offering, and Advanced Micro Devices, which launched its first AI rack called Helios in July. Cash is Nvidia’s other great advantage. The company generated $70 billion in free cash flow in the first half of this year, while AMD totaled just over $4 billion and Google parent Alphabet went cash flow negative in the second quarter to fund its buildout. That’s a big edge for Nvidia in building out its ecosystem. The company is now offering a full-service platform complete with software, services, integrated hardware and, for many customers, financing assistance. Nvidia’s most recent quarterly financial filing in August outlined over $500 billion in off-balance-sheet commitments over the coming years, with a majority maturing through fiscal 2029. That same month, Huang announced a partnership with six large asset managers on a $500 billion financing push designed to treat compute infrastructure as an asset class. That agreement, which promised financial firms up to $125 billion in residual value guarantees on GPU financings, was in addition to the stakes Nvidia has taken as a limited partner in private equity funds. The company seeded $2 billion in Brookfield’s inaugural AI Infrastructure Partners Fund, which aims to raise $10 billion in total capital, as well as other unconfirmed sums in KKR’s Helix Digital Infrastructure (an $11 billion vehicle) and Valor Equity Partners’ $5.4 billion dedicated compute fund. “We used to build chips that we sell, and these are technology components that people buy and use,” Huang told CNBC, in announcing the agreement in August. “But now, Nvidia’s AI factory platform is really an investable asset.” Huang has adopted a marketing mantra to reinforce the unique value of its equipment. “We’re the most rentable. We’re fungible, and we’re durable,” he said on a podcast with investor Brad Gerstner published last week. While Nvidia waits for Wall Street firms to pull in investors to expand the GPU loan pool, the chipmaker is already actively fostering record-sized deals in the AI infrastructure space. Nvidia’s biggest single guarantee is for OpenAI’s forthcoming facility in Pike County, Ohio, which could be the largest data center in the world. That deal requires use of Nvidia hardware for at least 20 years. The shift from chips to capital carries significant risks should OpenAI run into trouble. If OpenAI misses payments or faces insolvency, Nvidia can take over the lease, find a new tenant, or ask the landlord, SB Energy, to sell the facility, guaranteeing to pay the difference for the latter two arrangements up to $105 billion if the release or sale falls below a minimum price. Nvidia could also pay SB Energy a lump sum. On the other side, if OpenAI posts its own collateral, or achieves a high enough credit rating, Nvidia’s guarantee ends. At CoreWeave, Nvidia’s investment includes equity and a commitment to buy up to $6.3 billion of its compute if it can’t find another taker. Nvidia’s backstops can take many forms, such as guaranteeing a minimum resale price or a minimum hourly offtake price for the chips in the event the lender has to recoup the assets. With Sharon AI and other neoclouds, Nvidia’s deals have come with revenue-sharing agreements. “We believe these AI cloud partners have strong customer demand and robust sales pipelines but are constrained by the large-scale infrastructure that is required to meet that demand,” Nvidia said in its quarterly filing. Huang said this week that CoreWeave doesn’t need Nvidia’s backstop and that the neocloud’s cost of capital is decreasing. CoreWeave has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans. Yields on its bonds maturing in 2031 and 2032 topped 15%. Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said the market jitters reflect concerns about the stability of the business. CoreWeave and other neoclouds “will sign contracts into the future, and that all looks fine and dandy in their earnings reports, but is that contract going to be stable?” Stutland said. “Is it going to break at some point?” Nvidia says its financial support can help customers build the infrastructure needed to meet strong demand for its chips. More computing capacity could also help AI labs develop new models and services, creating further demand for Nvidia products. “They’ll do $700 billion in revenue next year,” Deepwater Asset Management founder Gene Munster told CNBC last month. “That affords them the ability to finance some of their customers.” Nvidia’s credit backstops have mostly kicked in over the past six to 12 months. Its last annual filing, published in February, makes no mention of AI cloud agreements. Warren Hosseinion, co-founder of AI infrastructure startup Compute Labs, said Nvidia doesn’t want to be in the position of insurer, “but they’re willing to play that role while the market and the industry catches up.” “They kind of control how things move,” said Hosseinion, whose company tokenizes GPUs in order to open up pools of capital for neocloud operators. “They have to be very careful about how they release their technology at what pace, because a lot of that will dictate how the market moves around it.” Nvidia is actively looking for insurers to bear some of the risk associated with the potential loss in value of GPUs. “Insurers are not yet a complete panacea to this problem,” said Tom Hoad, executive director of product innovation at global insurance group Howden. “But they are probably going to turn up and be helpful in the right situations, and therefore open up some commercial transactions.” According to research from New Constructs, Nvidia’s net present value of off-balance-sheet liabilities in fiscal 2026 totals over $153 billion, an increase of over $100 billion from last year. Such liabilities have been growing across the entire AI trade, mainly in the form of lease obligations. Ratings agencies like Moody’s have been sounding the alarm. In 2026, guarantees are the fastest-growing type of off-balance-sheet financing arrangements, the agency said. Moody’s doesn’t count guarantees as debt when rating corporate buyers, but it’s “something we’re constantly monitoring,” said David Gonzales, a vice president at the agency. “These things are advanced structures that are unique, and so there is no blanket real approach you can take,” he said. Gonzales said it’s likely that chips will retain “values in excess of contractual residual value amounts” in the near future, which would mitigate risk in many of Nvidia’s financing structures. Still, how much exposure investment grade AI players can handle is “the question we’re evaluating at all times every day,” Gonzales said. “It’s the center of all of our discussions right now,” he said. Lee compared the current environment with the late-1990s technology market, specifically pointing to Cisco Systems Inc.'s (CSCO) sharp decline in 1997 before the networking giant resumed its advance. He pointed out that Cisco experienced a major drawdown during this period as investors grappled with concerns over monetary policy and the sustainability of technology valuations. Lee added that a sharp correction did not prevent the broader technology investment cycle from continuing. Lee believes that the current cycle is similar to the one he mentioned above, adding that he sees opportunities in companies addressing AI infrastructure bottlenecks, memory stocks, Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) and the "Magnificent Seven". "I think the AI and the bottlenecks are the memories and the Nvidia's and the Mag 7. They're being sold because it is easy to short them now," he said. Beyond the major AI hardware names, Lee said he also likes software and cryptocurrency, while adding that there is potential for a broader cyclical move. Lee also argued that the AI infrastructure buildout remains enormous, estimating $30 trillion in spends over the next 25 years. He said the scale could ultimately make AI a more important infrastructure investment than previous major technology buildouts. During the after-hours session on Friday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 index, gained 0.15%; the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (QQQ) edged up by 0.07%; and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) rose 0.13%. title: TSMC or Nvidia: If I Could Only Own 1 for the Next 5 Years, It Would Be This 1. - The Motley Fool
content: You can't go wrong with either, but one seems to have more runway. The ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) boom has birthed many new inspiring companies, but it has also added a fresh spark to companies that have been around for decades. Many stocks have soared in recent years as investors pour money into AI stocks, but two of the main beneficiaries have been Nvidia (NVDA +2.39%) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +1.40%) (TSMC). In the past five years, Nvidia and TSMC are up 874% and 266%, respectively, far outperforming any major index. Both stocks are great options, but if you had to choose one, which should it be? Let's take a look. Nvidia is the poster child of the current AI boom, with its hardware (especially its GPUs) powering the most advanced AI models around. Nvidia's GPUs were initially used for video games, but they're also great at the processing required to train and run AI models. In its fiscal second quarter (ended July 26), Nvidia reported $96.2 billion in revenue (up 106% year over year), with $89 billion from its data center segment (up 117% year over year). Nvidia is more than just its advanced chips. It's done a great job of building a hardware-software ecosystem that essentially traps customers in because it's the de facto coding language used in AI development (called CUDA), and switching to a different chipmaker would be too costly and time-consuming for companies. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » This stronghold in enterprise AI is how Nvidia has become the world's most valuable public company, with a market cap of over $5.2 trillion (as of market open on Oct. 21). TSMC is the world's premier semiconductor (chip) foundry and is also extremely important to the AI ecosystem, but for a different reason. While companies like Nvidia design the chips they sell, TSMC manufactures them and brings them to life. None of TSMC's competitors can match its scale or capabilities, which is why it has long been the go-to for some of the world's top tech giants -- including Nvidia. When it comes to manufacturing advanced AI chips, TSMC has a monopoly, and that's putting it lightly. Being the go-to option has given TSMC significant pricing power, which it has used to its advantage. Its revenue growth is solid, but its margins are where its pricing power really shows up. From last third quarter to this recent third quarter, its gross margins rose from 59.5% to 66.4%, operating margin from 50.6% to 58.7%, and net profit margin from 45.7% to 51.1%. This should continue. During TSMC's latest earnings call, CEO C.C. Wei highlighted the demand, saying: The AI market continues to be very strong. Recent developments are very positive to AI's long-term demand outlook. We observe increasing AI demand, fueled by the rising adoption of agentic AI as we transition from chatbot to AI assistance. From a business standpoint, one reason I give TSMC the edge is because of how much Nvidia depends on it. Nvidia is a powerhouse, no doubt, but without TSMC's manufacturing ability, Nvidia's business becomes limited. It's at the mercy of TSMC's capacity and production timelines. TSMC is a great partner, but that dependency can also be a single point of failure. I don't see it happening, but the risk is there nonetheless. Nvidia could go with a rival like Samsung, but that could mean sacrificing production and having to redesign systems. The same concentration risk applies to many other tech companies. Regardless of who dominates the AI race between the AI hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms), they'll all rely on TSMC for manufacturing. That puts TSMC in a very lucrative position for at least the next five years, but even after the AI frenzy, it'll remain a key piece in the supply chain for tons of other electronics. From a stock standpoint, Nvidia and TSMC trade similarly, at 23.3 and 24.2 times their projected earnings next year, respectively. However, the difference in market caps ($5.2 trillion versus $2.2 trillion) leads me to believe that TSMC has more upside. It could double in value and still not be as valuable as Nvidia is now. We can't predict how any stock will perform, and you likely can't go wrong with investing in either stock. However, over the next five years, I like TSMC's upside. title: Memory Stocks Are Plummetting. Jensen Huang Says the Bears Have It Wrong. - The Motley Fool
content: The AI trade has looked awfully shaky over the last couple of weeks. CoreWeave, the neocloud company that may have more leveraged exposure to AI than any other company due to its massive debt burden, has plunged in recent weeks on fears over its rising debt yields. Memory stocks, which include Micron(MU +2.98%), SK Hynix (SKHY +4.09%), Samsung, and Sandisk (SNDK +1.42%), are also seen as some of the riskier AI stocks due to the cyclical nature of memory. Historically, memory chips have swung from gluts to shortages, with shortages lasting only two to three years on average. SK Hynix just pulled the planned IPO of its flash storage unit in the face of weak stock performance and investor interest, and Micron and its peers are trading down by roughly a third from their peak last July. That sell-off has come even as memory stocks have continued to report blockbuster results, and there's no evidence that the shortage is easing. The jitters seemed to reach a fever pitch earlier this month on fears that new products from China's leading memory chip company would compete with the established giants above. Nvidia (NVDA +2.39%) CEO Jensen Huang has stepped in to defend the AI sector many times, and now he's doing it with memory. At Nvidia's GTC Berlin conference, Huang said he doesn't expect an oversupply of memory until sometime after 2029, and explained about the supply-demand dynamic, "One of the things that's really great about memory is that you can always use more of it." He added that his company will continue to develop new ways to use memory to accelerate and improve performance. The value of a stock is supposed to represent the discounted value of future cash flows. In reality, it doesn't often work like that, as it's difficult to accurately predict future cash flows, and investor sentiment often makes stocks swing wildly, as is happening now. No one knows what the shape of the memory cycle looks like or for how long the shortage will endure. However, it does seem that margins, and therefore prices, are near their peak, which may be a sell signal to some. Micron reported a gross margin of 86.8% in its most recent quarter, and an operating margin of 80.7%, showing it kept more than four out of every five dollars it brought in in pre-tax profits. Few companies have ever reported an operating margin that high, which gives a sense of how extreme the pricing is in the memory market. For its next quarter, Micron called for a modest decline in gross margin to 85.95%. Realistically, there's probably little room for margins to go higher, and at a certain point, supply is as tight as it's going to get. The question now is how long the memory market will stay that way, and no one knows the answer. Using Micron as an example, I think memory stocks have gotten too cheap given their future profit potential, and the risk/reward profile leans toward long-term demand for memory growing as physical AI products like robotics and self-driving cars come to market. Micron now trades at a forward P/E of just 5. If it can sustain that level of profits for at least three years, then the valuation seems justified, especially with the potential to spend that cash on share buybacks. The long-term picture remains uncertain, but if the company can capitalize on the current windfall and approach paying back its valuation in just five years, then the stock is a buy no matter what happens in the 2030s.
